summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, in protests known locally as the Monsoon Revolution, is the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground afterwards, and trans people who had previously lived visibly now do so in hiding.

The current national incident baseline comes from JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across the country in 2025. The documented conduct includes murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend it has recorded since 2022.

Lethal violence against visible trans people is ongoing and recent. On 3 February 2025 the prominent trans advocate Shila, originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district. Five unidentified individuals are accused. Shila was widely known for humanitarian work, which makes the killing a direct measure of the risk attached to visibility.

Police contact is the most likely point of danger, and it is usually extortion-driven rather than prosecutorial. After hijras refused police demands for money in Gomdondi Phultala on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack. On 17 September 2025, police arrested twelve hijras who were collecting money from vehicles carrying expatriates, a traditional livelihood, in Narayanganj.

Policing of visibly trans people reaches transit hubs. In April 2024, five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, according to JMBF. An airport perimeter is therefore an actively policed site for trans people, not a neutral arrival point.

The legal baseline is the Penal Code 1860, which criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment. Outright International, updated 12 March 2026, records that the provision is rarely enforced through prosecution but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. A UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, issued September 2023 and updated April 2026, states that the scope of Section 377 remains ambiguous: it is unclear whether lesbianism falls within it, with ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report reading female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere treating the provision as relevant to all genders. Any visitor's conduct sits inside that ambiguity.

Formal recognition exists and does not translate into safety. Hijra are legally recognised as a third gender, with gender-marker change permitted, and Bangladesh has held LGBTIQ and hijra pride events since recognition was extended in 2013 and 2014. The gap between that status and the violence recorded in 2025 is the central finding of the Global Press Journal reporting, which profiles a trans subject who now lives in hiding.

Hostility tolerated by the state is documented at asylum-grade evidentiary standard. A UK Upper Tribunal decision, PA/07096/2017, relies on Home Office country material recording Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under Section 377 and under Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues. A Washington Blade assessment dated 5 August 2025, one year after the ouster, reaches the same conclusion in security terms: the LGBTQ community is increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.
tangentialFactors:
The contradiction between status and safety is the defining comparison inside the country. A rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021, and hijra pride events have been held in public, at a time when formal third-gender recognition was already a decade old. Both facts are drawn on by the same reporting that documents trans people going into hiding after 2024, so visibility gains of the previous decade should not be read as a current safety indicator.

The direction of travel since 2022 is documented rather than impressionistic: JMBF's own annual counts show a rising violation trend across four reporting years, with 2025 the sharpest single increase. Enforcement is concentrated on extortion, fabricated charges and arbitrary arrest rather than on conviction, which means the exposure a visitor faces is discretionary police action at street level.

The two external assessments date differently and should be read together. The UK Home Office country policy note was issued in September 2023, before the August 2024 change of government, and was updated in April 2026; the Washington Blade security assessment and the Global Press Journal field reporting both post-date the ouster and describe a worse environment than the legal note alone would suggest.

Comparable countries in the region also recognise third-gender categories in law, so legal recognition should not be treated as a proxy for regional safety either. The distinguishing feature here is the documented combination of a rarely enforced but broadly usable penal provision, an extortion economy organised around visibly trans people, and Islamist mobilisation that the state has not checked since 2024.

Twelve hijras were arrested on this basis in Narayanganj on 17 September 2025, and refusal to pay extortion demands preceded a retaliatory attack injuring at least twelve people in Gomdondi Phultala on 10 September 2025.

JMBF is the domestic body that compiles the national incident record. Its April 2026 report counts 260 violations against at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals for 2025, including murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion, and identifies the trend as rising since 2022.

outOfScopeNotes:
The reach of Section 377 toward lesbian conduct is unresolved in the sources. The UK Home Office country policy note, updated April 2026, records that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within the provision, and notes that ILGA's 2019 report is internally inconsistent on the point. No source resolves it.

Whether gender-marker change and third-gender registration remain administratively available in practice after August 2024 is not sourced. The sources confirm the legal provisions stand; none documents the current administrative process or any refusal to process applications.

The outcome for the five unidentified individuals accused in the killing of Shila on 3 February 2025 is unresolved. No source records an arrest, charge or trial result.

Nothing in the source inventory addresses entry or visa screening, border questioning of trans travellers, or whether foreign passport gender markers are recognised on arrival. Any statement on document screening at entry would be unsupported.

The extent to which the post-2024 government has changed official policy toward LGBTIQ people, as distinct from the security environment described by advocacy groups and journalists, is not sourced beyond the assessments cited here.
